objective: Graphic texts combine factual information and deliberate visual elements to communicate core messages; both components carry equal functional weight.；Graphic texts boost audience engagement, reduce reading time, improve long-term retention, and speed up pattern recognition for complex data.；Standard valid graphic text types include diagrams, flow charts, maps, visual articles, comparison charts, step-by-step sequences, and statistical displays.

learningGoals.statement: Understand the definition and benefits of graphic texts.
Apply the 4-step reading process for graphic texts.
Identify approved formats and originality requirements for Unit 1 Assignment 2.
Recognize the importance of graphic texts in real-world communication.

knowledgeNodes.name: Graphic Text Definition and Benefits
knowledgeNodes.definition: A graphic text is a communication tool that combines factual information (text, statistics) with deliberate visual elements; both components carry equal functional weight. Benefits include increased audience engagement, reduced reading time, improved long-term retention, and faster pattern recognition for complex datasets.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.

knowledgeNodes.name: 4-Step Graphic Text Reading Process
knowledgeNodes.definition: A structured approach to reading graphic texts: (1) Preview – scan overall structure, type, title, axis units; (2) Literal data extraction – locate explicit facts using labels, legends, keys; (3) Trend and relationship analysis – identify patterns, changes, connections; (4) Conclusion inference – combine extracted data with prior knowledge to draw overarching conclusions.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.

knowledgeNodes.name: Unit 1 Assignment 2 Graphic Text Creation
knowledgeNodes.definition: Students must create one original graphic text on a real-world topic using an approved format (visual article, comparison chart, map, statistical display, flow chart, or diagram; timelines prohibited) plus a 500-word minimum reflection. The work must be original; AI-generated, copied, or translated content is prohibited. Grading criteria: Knowledge (visual features), Inquiry (originality, planning), Communication (clarity, vocabulary), Application (grammar, reflection-design connection).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate the ability to use the writing process by generating and organizing ideas and producing first drafts, revised drafts, and final polished pieces to complete a variety of writing tasks.

knowledgeNodes.name: Reflection Component Requirements
knowledgeNodes.definition: The written reflection must be at least 500 words, structured as cohesive academic analysis (not bullet points), covering personal experience, challenges, core message clarity, and understanding of visual communication.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.

knowledgeNodes.name: Importance of Communication Skills
knowledgeNodes.definition: Understanding that communication skills (including reading and creating graphic texts) are essential in everyday life at school, work, and home. The lesson reinforces this by discussing real-world applications of graphic texts.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the importance of communication skills in their everyday lives - at school, at work, and at home.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects 'Timeline' as an allowed format in the diagnostic question.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think timelines are permitted for the assignment, but the lesson explicitly prohibits timelines.

miniLesson.explain: For Unit 1 Assignment 2, you must create an original graphic text using one of the approved formats: visual article, comparison/versus chart, map/floor plan, statistical data display, process flow chart, or structural diagram. Timelines are specifically NOT allowed. The lesson states: 'Timelines are prohibited.' Using a timeline will result in a mark of zero.
miniLesson.example: A student creates a timeline showing major events in Canadian history. This format is not permitted. Instead, the student could use a flow chart to show the sequence of events or a statistical display to show data over time.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: 'No timeline on the timeline!' – if you see the word 'timeline', it's not allowed.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an approved format for Unit 1 Assignment 2?
Your friend says, 'I'll use a timeline for my graphic text because it shows events in order.' Explain why this is incorrect and suggest an alternative approved format.
guidedPractice.answer: Timelines are prohibited. Your friend could use a flow chart to show the sequence of events, or a statistical display to present data over time.

guidedPractice.prompt: A classmate argues that a timeline should be allowed because it is a common graphic text type. Using course evidence, write a response that justifies why timelines are excluded and how this rule supports the learning goals of the assignment.
guidedPractice.answer: The lesson explicitly states 'Timelines are prohibited' under permitted formats. This rule ensures students focus on creating original graphic texts that require synthesis of visual and textual elements, such as visual articles or flow charts. The assignment aims to develop skills in combining factual information with deliberate visual design, not simply arranging dates in order.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks incorrect option on Q2 in diagnostic.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes visual elements in a graphic text are primarily decorative, rather than serving an equal functional role alongside factual information.

miniLesson.explain: In graphic texts, visual elements are not just decorative embellishments. They carry equal functional weight as the factual information, meaning both text and visuals are essential for communicating the core message. This is because visuals can enhance understanding, speed up pattern recognition, and improve retention. For example, a bar chart in a graphic about energy usage in Ontario shows data visually, making trends easier to grasp than a table of numbers alone.
miniLesson.example: Consider a graphic text about the Canadian forestry industry: it might combine a bar graph showing GDP contributions, a map of forest regions, and accompanying text. The visuals (graph, map) are not mere decoration; they convey key data and relationships that the text alone cannot achieve as efficiently.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Visuals are partners, not decorations – they carry equal weight with text.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the role of visual elements in a graphic text according to the lesson?
guidedPractice.answer: They carry equal functional weight alongside factual information.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student argues that visuals in graphic texts are just to make the page look nice. Explain why this is incorrect, using an example from the lesson.
guidedPractice.answer: This is incorrect because visuals are equally functional. For instance, in the energy usage graphic, the pie chart and bar graph present the data in a way that text alone cannot, making patterns like the relative proportions of energy sources immediately visible.

guidedPractice.prompt: Analyze the statement: 'In graphic texts, visuals are optional decorations.' How does this statement conflict with the lesson's definition? Provide reasoning and a counterexample.
guidedPractice.answer: The statement conflicts because the lesson defines graphic texts as combining factual information and deliberate visual elements with equal functional weight. If visuals were optional decorations, they could be removed without loss of meaning. However, removing the bar graph from a statistical display would remove essential data, making the graphic incomplete. Therefore, visuals are integral, not optional.

reteachModules.trigger: When a student selects that reading all fine print first is the best approach in a timed test, instead of previewing the overall structure.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Thinks that reading all details carefully is the best first step when approaching a graphic text, but the recommended strategy is to preview the structure first to map content locations.

miniLesson.explain: The 4-step standard reading process for graphic texts begins with Preview: scan the overall structure, type, title, and axis units. In timed tests, spend 10-30 seconds skimming headings and markers to map content locations, then directly look up specific sections for questions. This is more efficient than reading all details first, as it helps you locate explicit facts and analyze trends quickly.
miniLesson.example: Consider the Canadian forestry industry overview graphic (GDP, employment, assets). Instead of reading every number, preview the title, axis labels, and legend. Then, when asked about GDP, you immediately know where to look. This saves time and reduces cognitive load.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Preview first, details later. Like scanning a map before driving.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the first step in the 4-step reading process for graphic texts?
guidedPractice.answer: Preview – scan overall structure, type, title, axis units.

guidedPractice.prompt: You are given a bar graph showing energy usage in Ontario, 2013 (pie chart and bar graph). What should you do first in a timed test? Explain why.
guidedPractice.answer: First, preview the title, axis labels, and legend. This helps you locate specific data efficiently without getting lost in details.

guidedPractice.prompt: How does the preview step help with trend analysis and conclusion inference later? Use an example from the lesson.
guidedPractice.answer: By previewing, you understand the structure and can identify which data sets to compare. For example, previewing a comparison chart shows you the categories and variables, making it easier to spot trends like 'which category increased the most' and infer conclusions.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects 'A list of bullet points summarizing key points' as the required format for the reflection component.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes that bullet points are acceptable for the reflection, but the requirement is a cohesive academic paragraph or essay of at least 500 words.

miniLesson.explain: The reflection component of Unit 1 Assignment 2 must be written as a cohesive academic paragraph or essay, not as a bullet-point list. It must be at least 500 words and cover personal experience, challenges, core message clarity, and understanding of visual communication. The reflection is a formal piece of writing, not a list of notes.
miniLesson.example: For instance, a correct reflection might begin: 'Creating my graphic text on renewable energy sources taught me how visual elements can enhance data comprehension. I faced challenges in selecting appropriate colors to convey urgency…' This is a flowing paragraph, not a set of bullet points.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Reflection = essay, not list. Aim for 500+ words of connected prose.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the minimum word count required for the reflection?
Which of the following best describes the required format for the reflection? (A) A series of bullet points, (B) A cohesive academic paragraph or essay.
A student submits a reflection with three bullet points: '• Learned about graphic texts • Used colors to show trends • Reflection is 300 words'. What are two errors in this submission?
guidedPractice.answer: 1) The reflection is in bullet-point format instead of cohesive prose; 2) It is only 300 words, but the minimum is 500 words.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects an option indicating that reusing a pre-existing graphic without recombination is acceptable.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think that using a pre-existing graphic from the internet or a textbook without significant original recombination is acceptable for the assignment.

miniLesson.explain: While you may reuse clip art and pre-existing images, the graphic text must be originally created by you. This means you cannot simply copy a graphic from another source. You must combine clip art elements into a new, original layout that communicates your own message. The assignment specifically prohibits AI generation, copying, translation tools, or third-party assistance. Violation results in an automatic zero.
miniLesson.example: A student who copies an existing infographic from a website and submits it as-is is not allowed. Another student selects clip art images of a tree, a factory, and a graph, arranges them into a new infographic about deforestation impacts, and adds original text – that meets the originality requirement.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Create, don't copy: Your graphic text must be a new combination of elements, not a borrowed image.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following actions would meet the originality requirement? A) Copying a diagram from a textbook B) Recombining clip art into a new layout C) Using an AI-generated image D) Taking a screenshot from a video
You want to create a graphic text about renewable energy. You found a perfect bar chart online. What should you do to meet the originality requirement?
guidedPractice.answer: You should not use the bar chart directly. Instead, create your own chart using data you research, or recombine clip art of wind turbines, solar panels, etc. into a new visual layout.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain in your own words why the assignment requires original creation and not simply reusing a pre-existing graphic. Include the potential consequences of violating the rule.
guidedPractice.answer: The assignment requires original creation to demonstrate our own understanding and planning skills. Reusing a pre-existing graphic would not show our own work. Violating the rule results in a zero for the assignment. We can use clip art, but we must recombine it into a new layout that is our own.

cards.question: According to the lesson, what is the role of visual elements in a graphic text?
options: They are primarily decorative to make the text look attractive.
They carry equal functional weight alongside factual information.
They replace the need for any written text.
They are used only in statistical displays.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of the functional weight of visuals.
misconceptions: Visuals carry equal functional weight, not just decoration.
✓ 正确
Visuals enhance but do not replace text.
Visuals appear in many graphic text types.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that visuals are equally functional.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.

cards.question: What is the recommended first step when reading a graphic text in a timed test?
options: Read all the fine print and data labels carefully.
Skim the overall structure, title, and axis units to map content.
Immediately look for the answer to the question.
Count the number of visual elements.

misconceptions: The recommended first step is to preview the structure, not dive into details.
